children: By Portia Crowe and AyenDeng Bior
Senegal's finances have been in crisis since the 2024 discovery of billions of dollars in debt, hidden by a government no longer in charge of the West African country.
Following is a timeline of how Senegal's debt woes unfolded and efforts to address them:
March 2024 – Opposition candidate Bassirou Diomaye Faye, a former tax inspector popular with young voters, wins the presidential election.
September 2024 – Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko accuses former President Macky Sall's government of lying to partners and falsifying figures.

October 2024 – Moody's downgrades Senegal's long-term ratings to B1 from Ba3. An IMF mission begins assessing the impact of revised fiscal data on past and current lending programmes and suspends Senegal's $1.8 billion credit facility.
November 2024 – Faye and Sonko's Pastef party wins parliamentary elections, giving them a mandate for promised reforms.

February 2025 – The Court of Auditors confirms Sall's government understated debt and deficit figures, pegging end-2023 debt at 99.7% of GDP, well above previously reported 74.41%, implying hidden borrowing of around $7 billion. Senegal says it will investigate alleged malfeasance and targets a new IMF programme by June.
March 2025 – The IMF says new programme talks cannot proceed until debt misreporting is addressed. It urges Senegal to streamline tax exemptions and phase out costly energy subsidies.

June 2025 – Sonko says Senegal will boost tax compliance to raise revenue and cut reliance on external financing. Finance ministry data show public debt had climbed by end-March. Banks estimate the new figures push debt-to-GDP to 119%.
July 2025 – S&P Global Ratings downgrades the long-term sovereign rating to "B-", pegging hidden debts at around $13 billion.
August 2025 – Sonko announces an economic recovery plan funded 90% by domestic resources and pledges to avoid new external debt.

November 2025 – The IMF concludes a mission without a new lending programme. Some international bonds hit record lows. Sonko says the IMF is pushing Dakar to restructure, which would be a "disgrace". S&P downgrades Senegal to "CCC+" from "B-".

December 2025 – The IMF says it made "significant progress" toward a new programme while continuing internal investigation into how it failed to detect the unreported debt. Finance Minister Cheikh Diba tells lawmakers the IMF discussions are "going very well" and they hope to finalise a programme "very quickly."
January 2026 – Prime Minister Sonko says Senegal will not need to restructure debt.
February 2026 – Finance Minister Diba tells lawmakers "fundamental differences" remain with the IMF. The IMF says corrective measures related to the misreporting have been agreed.
March 2026 – Senegal makes $480 million in payments to international bondholders. Diba defends the government's use of total return swaps and pushes back against accusations of a lack of disclosure.
April 2026 – Senegal's economy ministry says growth is expected to slow to 2.5% in 2026 from 6.7% in 2025. The IMF cuts its 2026 growth forecast to 2.2%.

May 2026 – Diba tells lawmakers the fuel subsidy bill could exceed its 2026 budget allocation by up to $2 billion and says Faye had proposed an alternative to restructuring to the IMF's Georgieva. Faye sacks Sonko and dissolves the government and names economist Ahmadou Al Aminou Lo as prime minister. Parliament then elects Sonko as its speaker.
June 2026 – The IMF says a mission the week of June 15 in Dakar will continue technical discussions with authorities.

September 2026 – The ​IMF and Senegal reach a staff-level agreement ‌for a three-year, $2.2 billion loan package that requires the West African country seek creditors' relief. The agreement is subject to approval by the IMF Executive Board. Senegal's ministry of economy and finance separately says it agreed to an "enhanced common framework" to restore debt sustainability.
